title: Attainment Grouping and the EEF/UCL Report: Choose Your Casualty
author: The Disruptive Educator
summary: The Disruptive Educator critically analyzes a major Education Endowment Fund and UCL Institute of Education report on student grouping in mathematics, arguing that every grouping model creates instructional casualties among different student populations.
points: The EEF/UCL study involving nearly 15,000 students found that streaming benefits high-prior-attaining students while low-prior-attaining students make similar progress in either model.
Mixed-attainment classrooms tend to be paced more similarly to bottom-set classes, leaving high-attainers as instructional casualties despite being in an ostensibly inclusive model.
Research on streaming is confounded by multiple uncontrollable variables including teaching quality, curriculum exposure, teacher expertise allocation, and school culture.
"Instructional casualties" are students failed in their learning due to poor instruction. Every grouping model creates different casualties.
Teacher expertise allocation is underutilized in streaming decisions. Expert teachers should work with low-prior-attainers who have furthest to go in knowledge development.
quotes: Every way we group students simultaneously solves and creates problems for different learners.
When we try to run experiments on student grouping, we are studying grouping tangled up with curriculum delivery, teacher expertise, school culture, and student behavior.
The students who most need exposure to the content get less of it, and they're the least likely to land upon the correct answer alone.
The uncomfortable truth is that every grouping model can create tradeoffs.
